references.text: Isaiah's parable of the vineyard where God has done everything for his vineyard and expects fruit. When the vineyard does not bear fruit, he threatens judgment – the same theme as the fig tree that gets one last chance to bear fruit. [ref:Jes 5:2-4|Isaiah 5:2-4]

The immediate context: the parable of the barren fig tree where the vineyard owner asks for one more year to fertilize and care for the tree, before verse 9 gives the final condition – either it bears fruit or it is cut down. [ref:Luk 13:6-8|Luke 13:6-8]

John the Baptist's warning that the axe is already lying at the root of the trees, and every tree that does not bear good fruit will be cut down and thrown into the fire – the same image of judgment over barrenness. [ref:Luk 3:9|Luke 3:9]
Parallel to Luke 3:9 in Matthew: every tree that does not bear good fruit is cut down. The image of cutting down the tree (ἐκκόπτω) is the same as in Luke 13:9. [ref:Matt 3:10|Matthew 3:10]

Jesus uses the same image in the Sermon on the Mount: every tree that does not bear good fruit is cut down and thrown into the fire. It underscores the consequences of failing to bear fruit. [ref:Matt 7:19|Matthew 7:19]

Jesus curses the barren fig tree, and it withers. A dramatic act illustrating judgment on Israel for lack of fruit – thematically closely related to the parable in Luke 13. [ref:Matt 21:19|Matthew 21:19]

Jesus speaks about the branches on the vine: whoever does not bear fruit is cut off, while whoever bears fruit is cleansed to bear more. The same principle of fruitfulness as a condition for continued life. [ref:Joh 15:2-4|John 15:2-4]

Land that drinks the rain and produces useful crops receives blessing. But land that produces thorns and thistles is worthless and in danger of being cursed and burned – parallel to the barren fig tree. [ref:Hebr 6:7-8|Hebrews 6:7-8]

The Lord is patient and does not want anyone to perish, but that all should come to repentance. God's patience in giving the fig tree another year reflects this principle of a time of grace. [ref:2 Pet 3:9|2 Peter 3:9]

Paul asks whether one despises God's riches of kindness, forbearance, and patience, not understanding that God's kindness leads to repentance. The fig tree gets an extra chance – God's patience calling for repentance. [ref:Rom 2:4|Romans 2:4]
